question_text:
In the 1950s, engineers at the Kessmar Aerodynamics Laboratory placed scale models of chimneys and cooling towers in a wind tunnel to study how air vortices peel away from their sides. The knowledge the engineers gained from these tests of slender, wind-excited towers ______ the design of nearly every tall chimney built since.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: Choice B is the best answer. The convention being tested is subject-verb agreement. The subject of the sentence is the singular noncount noun "knowledge," which is followed by a relative clause with "that" omitted ("[that] the engineers gained from these tests of slender, wind-excited towers"). The nouns "engineers," "tests," and "towers" sit inside that clause, so they don't determine the number of the main verb. The singular verb "has shaped" agrees with "knowledge," and its present perfect form, signaled by "since," fits a period of influence that began in the 1950s and continues to the present ("every tall chimney built since").
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect because the plural verb "have shaped" doesn't agree in number with the singular subject "knowledge." It is drawn toward the nearby plural nouns "tests" and "towers," which are part of a modifier and are not the subject of the sentence.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect because "shaping" is a present participle, a non-finite verb form, and cannot serve as the main verb of the sentence. With it, the subject "The knowledge ..." has no finite verb, which results in a sentence fragment.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect because the pronoun "it" repeats the subject. The noun phrase "The knowledge the engineers gained ..." already serves as the subject of the verb, so adding "it" creates a redundant, ungrammatical double subject.

question_text:
Reconstructing the nightly flight paths of migrating songbirds from the faint echoes recorded by coastal weather radars ______ careful filtering of the signals that rain, insects, and ground clutter also produce before any track can be drawn.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: Choice C is the best answer. The convention being tested is subject-verb agreement. The subject of the sentence is the gerund phrase "Reconstructing the nightly flight paths of migrating songbirds from the faint echoes recorded by coastal weather radars." A gerund phrase names a single activity, so it is singular no matter how many plural nouns appear inside it or just before the blank. The sentence needs a singular finite main verb, and "requires" supplies it; the phrase "careful filtering of the signals ..." then serves as the verb's object.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect because the plural verb "require" doesn't agree in number with the singular gerund-phrase subject "Reconstructing ... radars." It agrees only with the nearby plural noun "radars," which sits inside the subject phrase and is not the subject of the sentence.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect because the participle "requiring" is a non-finite verb form and can't serve as the main verb of the sentence. With it, the sentence has no finite verb in its main clause, which results in a sentence fragment, since the only finite verbs, "produce" and "can be drawn," appear in subordinate clauses.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect because the pronoun "it" is a redundant second subject. The gerund phrase "Reconstructing ... radars" is already the subject of the sentence, so adding "it" before the verb repeats that subject and results in an ungrammatical construction.

question_text:
Astronomers have monitored the five rocky planets orbiting the red dwarf Selvik-7 for years, and the spectra of four of them remain featureless. Selvik-7d is the only one of these planets that, since 2019, ______ a detectable trace of water vapor in its atmosphere during transit observations.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: Choice A is the best answer. The convention being tested is subject-verb agreement in a relative clause, along with verb tense. The relative pronoun "that" is the subject of the clause containing the blank, and a relative pronoun takes the number of its antecedent. Here the antecedent is "the only one," not "planets": the phrase "the only one" tells us that exactly one planet has the property, and "of these planets" merely names the group that one is drawn from. The antecedent is singular, so the verb must be singular. In addition, "since 2019," which sits inside the same clause as the blank, marks a period that began in the past and continues to the present, which calls for the present perfect. "Has shown" is singular and present perfect, so it is the only choice that fits.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect because "have shown" is a plural verb. The relative pronoun "that" refers to "the only one," which is singular, not to the plural noun "planets" that sits closer to it. This is the opposite of the familiar pattern "one of the planets that have ..."; with "the only one," the verb must be singular.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect because the simple past tense "showed" does not fit the time frame set by "since 2019" in the same clause. When "since" introduces a starting point and the period runs up to the present, the verb must be in the present perfect ("has shown"), not the simple past.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect because "showing" is a participle, not a finite verb. The relative pronoun "that" needs a finite verb (one with tense) in its clause, and "showing" supplies none, so the relative clause is ungrammatical.

question_text:
Written over six years of interviews with salt-pan workers, midwives, and long-haul truck drivers along the Kutch coast, poet Kavitha Ilango's book-length poem "Letters from the Salt Flats" ______ the lives of three generations as a single unbroken sequence, unlike her first book, a collection of discrete lyrics.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: Choice B is the best answer. The convention being tested is subject-verb agreement. The subject of the sentence is the singular noun "poem" ("poet Kavitha Ilango's book-length poem"), and the title "Letters from the Salt Flats" simply renames that poem. Although the title is plural in form, it doesn't change the number of the subject. The plural nouns "workers," "midwives," and "drivers" belong to the introductory modifier and likewise don't determine the verb's number. The singular verb "traces" agrees with "poem."
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect because the plural verb "trace" doesn't agree in number with the singular subject "poem." It is drawn toward the plural-looking title "Letters from the Salt Flats" and the plural nouns in the introductory modifier, none of which is the subject.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect because the nonfinite participle "tracing" cannot serve as the main verb of the sentence. Used here, it leaves the subject "poem" without a finite verb and results in a sentence fragment.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect because it results in a redundant subject. The subject of the sentence, "poem," has already been stated, so adding the pronoun "it" gives the verb a second subject and is ungrammatical.

question_text:
When highway engineers surveyed the sinkholes and caverns beneath the Orrenvale Plateau's limestone ridges in 1998, they were surprised to find most of the caverns dry despite the region's heavy rainfall. Equally surprising to the engineers who mapped those ridges and caverns ______ the near-total absence of surface streams in the region's valleys.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: Choice A is the best answer. The convention being tested is subject-verb agreement in an inverted sentence. The second sentence opens with the adjective phrase "Equally surprising to the engineers who mapped those ridges and caverns," and the true subject, "the near-total absence of surface streams," comes after the verb. Because the head noun "absence" is singular, the verb must be singular. The plural nouns "engineers," "ridges," and "caverns" come before the blank, but they belong to the fronted phrase and aren't the subject. "Was" is singular and matches the past-tense narration ("surveyed," "found," "mapped").
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect because the plural verb "were" doesn't agree in number with the singular subject "absence." The plural nouns "engineers," "ridges," and "caverns" come right before the blank, but they are part of the fronted phrase; the subject follows the verb.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect because "it was" adds a second, redundant subject. Then "the near-total absence of surface streams" is left with no verb of its own, and the opening phrase "Equally surprising to the engineers who mapped those ridges and caverns" has nothing to modify. The sentence needs the verb alone so that "the near-total absence of surface streams" can serve as its subject.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect because "being" is a nonfinite participle, not a finite verb. Used here, it leaves the second sentence without a main verb, which results in a sentence fragment.

question_text:
Before the Tavish Delta's upstream dams were completed in 1968, roughly two-thirds of the sediment that the region's rivers carried from the surrounding highlands ______ down on the delta's coastal marshes, where it offset the land lost each year to erosion and subsidence.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: Choice D is the best answer. The convention being tested is subject-verb agreement, along with verb tense and verb form. The subject of the sentence is the fraction "two-thirds," and the phrase "of the sediment" tells the reader what the fraction refers to. "Sediment" is a noncount (mass) noun, so the fraction takes a singular verb even though "two-thirds" sounds plural and the nouns "rivers" and "highlands" nearer the blank are plural. Because the passage places the action before 1968 ("Before the Tavish Delta's upstream dams were completed in 1968"), the verb must also be in a past tense. "Was laid" is a singular past-tense passive verb that agrees with the subject and uses the correct participle of the transitive verb "lay," which means to set something down.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect because "has been laid" is in the present perfect tense, which links a past action to the present. The introductory clause places the action before the dams were completed in 1968, so the verb must be in the past tense, and the present perfect conflicts with that time cue.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect because "lain" is the past participle of the intransitive verb "lie," which cannot take a direct object and therefore cannot be used in the passive voice. The sediment is something that was set down by the rivers, so the passive form requires the participle of the transitive verb "lay," which is "laid."
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect because the plural verb "were" doesn't agree in number with the subject. When a fraction is followed by "of" and a noncount noun such as "sediment," the verb is singular; the plural nouns "rivers" and "highlands" closer to the blank are not what the verb must agree with.

question_text:
Since its founding in 1961 as a test of navigational endurance across the Kelthorn Fells, the Ravelstane Orienteering Trial has awarded its silver compass, the oldest trophy on the regional circuit, to ______ completes the full forty-kilometer course without relying on a handheld GPS unit.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: Choice C is the best answer. The convention being tested is pronoun case in a clause that functions as the object of a preposition. The preposition "to" does not take a lone pronoun here; it takes the entire clause "______ completes the full forty-kilometer course." Within that clause, the blank is the subject of the verb "completes," so the pronoun must be in the subjective case. "Whoever" is subjective and also stands for the unnamed recipient of the trophy, so it makes the clause a noun clause that can serve as the object of "to." The case of the pronoun is decided by its job inside its own clause, not by the preposition that comes before the clause.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect because "whomever" is in the objective case, but the blank is the subject of "completes," and a subject requires the subjective case. The preposition "to" governs the whole clause, not the pronoun inside it, so it does not make the objective form appropriate here.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect because "who" is a relative pronoun that needs an antecedent noun to modify, and the text supplies none after "to." Without a word such as "whoever" or "anyone," the clause "who completes the full forty-kilometer course" cannot serve as the object of the preposition "to."
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect because "those who" is plural, but the verb "completes" is singular. A relative pronoun takes the number of its antecedent, so "those who" would require the plural verb "complete," and the result does not agree in number.
